Eggs of Xiphias gladius hatch after approximately 3 days [ab = approximately 3 days] when incubated at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a brief developmental period consistent with the warm, pelagic spawning grounds this species frequents. Newly emerged prolarvae measure roughly 0.4 cm [Lb = roughly 0.4 cm] in total length, although the bill itself is already apparent at about 1 mm. This minute size places the hatchling among the smallest of large pelagic teleosts, reflecting the high fecundity strategy that characterizes the species. The wet weight at birth, derived from the allometric scaling of body dimensions, is approximately 0.001661 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.001661 grams], a value that underscores the minute energetic investment per offspring, a common strategy among high-fecundity pelagic spawners. These early life stages drift as ichthyoplankton in warm surface waters, where predation pressure is intense and rapid growth is essential for survival. The yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the first few days post-hatching, with the transition to exogenous feeding occurring once the mouth gapes and retinal differentiation permits prey detection.

As the juvenile swordfish grows, its body proportions undergo a dramatic allometric shift, most notably in the elongation of the bill and the deepening of the caudal peduncle. A common index of size in fisheries science is the lower jaw-to-fork length (LJFL), which can be estimated from the fork length using the relationship LJFL equals fork length minus 20.6207, all divided by 1.4847; for this species, the ultimate LJFL reaches approximately 292.6 centimeters [Li = approximately 292.6 centimeters]. For a fully grown adult, this asymptotic length can be substantial; the maximum recorded wet weight for the species reaches approximately 650,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 650,000 grams], placing X. gladius among the heaviest of the billfishes. Such an ultimate body mass is not attained quickly, however, as growth rates decelerate markedly once the fish surpasses several hundred kilograms. The species exhibits a relatively fast early growth phase, with individuals investing heavily in somatic tissue before diverting resources toward reproductive structures. Comparative studies with other istiophorid billfishes indicate that swordfish achieve a larger asymptotic size than most marlins and sailfish, likely due to differences in foraging ecology and thermal habitat preferences.

Puberty in Xiphias gladius is attained at a lower jaw-to-fork length of 168.2 centimeters [Lp = 168.2 centimeters], a size that typically corresponds to an age of several years for both sexes. However, the wet weight at puberty differs markedly between males and females; females reach reproductive maturity at approximately 74,000 grams [Wwp = approximately 74,000 grams], whereas males mature at a considerably smaller 21,000 grams [Wwp = 21,000 grams]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in size at maturity suggests that females require a longer period of somatic growth before initiating gametogenesis, a pattern common among pelagic fishes where fecundity is strongly correlated with body size. Histological examination of gonadal tissue has revealed that the onset of vitellogenesis in females coincides with the attainment of this size threshold, while males exhibit active spermatogenesis well before reaching comparable body masses. The divergence likely reflects differing selective pressures on the sexes: larger females produce more numerous and larger eggs, enhancing larval survival, whereas male reproductive success is more closely tied to access to spawning females rather than absolute body size.

Reproductive output in swordfish is among the highest of any teleost, with a single large female capable of releasing between 1 and 29 million eggs per spawn [N_R_i = between 1 and 29 million eggs per spawn]. Under the thermal conditions typical of tropical spawning aggregations at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], females may spawn multiple times during a breeding season, with an estimated frequency of approximately once every 24 days [F_R_i = multiple times during a breeding season, with an estimated frequency of approximately once every 24 days]. This yields a daily maximum reproductive rate that ranks among the highest for any marine fish species, a life-history strategy that compensates for extremely high early-life mortality in the plankton. Interestingly, this age at first reproduction is comparatively late for a species with such high fecundity, suggesting that the energetic benefits of continued somatic growth outweigh the advantages of earlier breeding in the competitive oceanic environment where annual survival is low for small individuals.

Maximum lifespan in swordfish is estimated at 11 years [am = 11 years] in the wild, a value obtained from mark-recapture studies and validated by otolith microincrement analysis conducted at an average water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This longevity, while modest compared to some deepwater teleosts, is considerable for a highly migratory species that undergoes extensive transoceanic movements and supports major commercial fisheries. The species' life history is characterized by a relatively rapid turnover: hatchlings that survive the perilous larval phase grow quickly through the juvenile stage, reach puberty by 4.5 years after hatching [tR = 4.5 years after hatching], and reproduce repeatedly over a reproductive lifespan of roughly six years before senescence sets in at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Natural mortality rates are highest during the first year of life, when the prolarvae are vulnerable to predation by gelatinous zooplankton and small pelagic fishes, but once individuals surpass approximately 168.2 centimeters [Lp = approximately 168.2 centimeters] in LJFL, the risk of natural death declines substantially. The interplay between early-life mortality and the energetic demands of long-distance migration has shaped the species' characteristic fast-growth, high-fecundity strategy, which contrasts with the slower-paced life histories observed in many deep-sea teleosts of comparable body size.
